source_events.evidence:
Our first public model is **Jev**, available today in early access. Jev achieves similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs, while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient. While Jev gives up string generation, it’s optimized for structured outputs and _can’t_ hallucinate.

source_events.title: Jev with coding agents
source_events.evidence:
Jev is a [System One model](/concepts/system-one). It does not generate text, write code, or hold a conversation. It takes a [state](/concepts/state) and a set of typed [questions](/primitives) and returns structured answers your code can use directly:

* A `choice` from a list of options, with per-option probabilities.
* A `score` on a rubric you define.
* A `noul` (0–1) for a true/false statement.

Coding agents rely on an LLM that streams text, calls tools, and edits files based on natural-language instructions. Jev does none of that. There is no `model: "jev-latest"` setting that turns your coding agent into a Jev-powered agent, because the two systems solve different problems.

source_events.title: Jev 1.13 jaggedness
source_events.evidence:
`jev-1.13` is fast, calibrated, and good at common-sense judgment but it is not perfect. `jev-1.13` does the best on [System One](/concepts/system-one) tasks. It may struggle with tasks that require additional levels of indirection. It can be quite literal in its understanding. It struggles with tasks that require numeric precision.
Jev is not a calculator. We strongly recommend implementing any mathematical logic in code. Jev will perform better on semantic questions than mathematical ones.
Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision. Unrelated detail acts as a distractor, and a large state makes it harder to tell which part of the input produced a wrong answer.

source_events.title: About Copilot auto model selection
source_events.evidence:
Auto model selection with task optimization combines two systems to provide high quality results and better reliability. One system tracks real-time system health and availability, while the other evaluates task complexity. Putting these together, auto model selection routes the task to the optimal model.
When you select **Auto**, auto model selection chooses from supported models, subject to your policies and subscription type. Available models may change over time.
For each prompt, the model is selected by considering cost, quality, and latency, to provide cost effective and efficient performance appropriate to the complexity of each prompt.

source_events.title: Jev Golden-Set Accuracy Study
source_events.evidence:
## Headline results

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Relevance accuracy (0–2 rubric, rounded to level, vs labeled band) | **22/25 = 88%** |
| Credibility accuracy (0–2 rubric, rounded to level, vs labeled level) | **24/25 = 96%** |
| Mean answer confidence | 0.77 |
| Items | 25 |
| Rubric version | 1.1.0 (pinned in `src/judge.ts`) |
| Model access | `typesafe-ai/jev` via Vercel AI Gateway (`/v4/ai/evaluation-model`) |
| Cost of the full run | ~$0.0001 (free-window pricing; ~$0.042/M input regardless) |

## Caveats, honestly

- n=25 is small; a single item is a 4-point swing. This is a calibration
  smoke test, not a benchmark.
- Single run; free-tier access, model version not pinnable through the
  Gateway (no version metadata is exposed).
- Labels are one person-session's judgment; two of the four misses are
  plausibly label/rubric artifacts rather than model errors, which cuts both
  ways.
- Rubric wording materially affects results (that's the point of pinning it);
  our v1.1.0 wording provably diverges from label intent on two items.

narration:
Production note: This episode uses AI-generated narration.

Here is the recommendation first: do not adopt Jev as a new everyday Copilot model. You cannot select it as a native Copilot chat model, and it cannot replace Sol, Astra, Claude, Gemini, or any other model that writes code and explains its reasoning. If you have a repeated classification, risk-scoring, or routing step, Jev is worth a small measured experiment. Otherwise, skip it for now.

TypeSafe calls it a “System One” model. You send it some state — text or structured data — plus narrowly typed questions. It returns one of three shapes: a choice from options you provide, a score against a rubric, or a probability for a yes-or-no statement. It does not generate prose. It does not write code. It does not maintain a conversation. TypeSafe’s own coding-agent guide says explicitly that Jev is not a drop-in replacement for Copilot or another coding agent.

The latest stable release documented today is Jev 1.13. The official price is four-point-two cents per million input tokens, with outputs free. The documented context limit is sixty-four thousand tokens per request. Pricing, latency, and benchmark comparisons can change and remain vendor measurements, not a guarantee for your workload.

There is also an important correction to the launch phrase “can’t hallucinate.” Jev cannot emit an invented free-form answer outside the schema, because there is no free-form answer. That is a genuine interface advantage. It does not mean every typed judgment is correct. TypeSafe’s own jaggedness page says version 1.13 can be too literal, struggles with numeric precision and indirection, degrades when the state is cluttered, and should leave arithmetic and deterministic checks to code. Type-safe means schema-valid, not truth-safe.

So, can you choose Jev from the model picker in VS Code Copilot Chat? No. GitHub’s current supported-model list does not include Jev, and TypeSafe says there is no Jev setting that turns a coding agent into a Jev-powered agent. Copilot’s Auto mode selects among Copilot-supported chat models based on task complexity, policy, availability, cost, and latency. Jev is not part of that pool.

What about Bring Your Own Key? VS Code can add compatible language-model endpoints using Chat Completions, Responses, or Anthropic Messages APIs. Jev exposes a different evaluation endpoint and does not generate chat responses. So pointing VS Code’s custom-endpoint model picker directly at Jev is not a supported fit. A model-provider extension could theoretically wrap it, but it would still need to synthesize conversational output, defeating the core product boundary.

The practical route is to keep Copilot’s normal host model and expose Jev as a tool. VS Code supports local or remote MCP servers, and the chat model can invoke their tools. But that tool call does not change the selected chat model. Sol or Astra remains the agent that reads the request, decides whether to call a tool, and explains or edits afterward. Jev only supplies a bounded judgment inside that larger turn.

TypeSafe publishes an official agent skill that teaches coding agents how to build against the API. That skill is documentation, not an MCP server. I did not find an official TypeSafe MCP server in the official documentation index or the company’s GitHub organization. I did find community servers. One prominent proof of concept, `jkudish/jev-mcp`, exposes several bounded judgment tools and documents a local Node-based M-C-P configuration. It is explicitly a community repository, not an official TypeSafe integration. I did not install or run it, so treat this as a route to inspect, not a tested recommendation.

For a practical workflow, the best pilot is not “let Jev help me code.” It is narrower. Imagine an issue-triage tool that first applies deterministic rules, then asks Jev to choose a category, score operational risk, and estimate whether human review is needed. Copilot stays responsible for investigation, explanation, and code changes. Application code validates the result, applies thresholds, and records the model version. Low-confidence or high-impact cases go to a person or a stronger reasoning model.

A second candidate is research intake: score fetched items for relevance and credibility before the expensive host model reads them. There is one small independent study of this exact shape. It reported eighty-eight percent relevance accuracy and ninety-six percent credibility accuracy on twenty-five hand-labeled search results. That is encouraging, but the sample is tiny, labels came from one person-session, and rubric wording changed two apparent outcomes. It is a smoke test, not a benchmark.

Compare that with the alternatives before adding anything. Deterministic rules win when the condition is actually deterministic. A small chat model with structured outputs may already be good enough if you need explanation, extraction, or generation in the same call. Copilot Auto already reduces manual model selection for normal chat tasks. Jev’s incremental value appears when the same narrow semantic judgment happens often enough that lower latency, typed distributions, and explicit confidence can repay the extra integration.

That integration is not free. Every use adds a tool round trip on top of the host model’s turn, separate TypeSafe billing and credentials, and another availability dependency. Text sent to the tool leaves the Copilot boundary and goes to TypeSafe. TypeSafe says it does not train on customer input, but its privacy policy also says it collects service input and may retain personal data as reasonably necessary; zero-data-retention is described as an enterprise option. Do not send private repository content until those terms and your threat model are acceptable. And VS Code warns that local MCP servers can run arbitrary code, so source-review and pin any server you install.

Here is a reproducible pilot. Pick one bounded classification lane with at least two hundred previously resolved examples. Freeze the Jev version, rubric, and thresholds. Compare four paths: deterministic rules, your current small structured-output model, Jev alone, and Jev with low-confidence escalation. Measure task accuracy, calibration by confidence band, false-positive cost, end-to-end latency including Copilot’s tool round trip, token cost, failure rate, and review volume. Keep a holdout set and test adversarial and ambiguous cases. Adopt only if Jev produces a clear quality, latency, or cost win after integration overhead — not merely valid JSON.

The bottom line: experiment, narrowly. Jev is a potentially useful decision primitive beside Copilot, not another model inside Copilot. For ordinary coding chat, it is redundant and less capable. For high-volume, typed semantic gates where deterministic rules stop working, it may be genuinely differentiated. Prove that on your own data before making it infrastructure.
show_notes:
# Show notes — Jev and Copilot: a specialist, not a replacement

Original production research cutoff: 2026-09-23 06:15 EDT (10:15 UTC).
Later evidence snapshot review: captures at 2026-09-23 15:17 UTC; reviewed at 15:17:26 UTC. This later review updates only these written publication notes; the original transcript, audio, source-event dates, and production notes remain historical inputs.

## Recommendation

Experiment narrowly; do not adopt Jev as an everyday Copilot chat model.

Jev is a typed decision model for bounded classification, scoring, and yes/no judgments. It is not a conversational or coding model, is not on GitHub Copilot’s current native model list, and is not eligible for Copilot Auto. The plausible VS Code route is to retain a supported Copilot host model and let it call Jev through a reviewed tool integration. No integration was installed or tested for this episode.

## What is documented

- Jev takes state plus typed questions and returns Choice, Score, or Noul results, including distributions and confidence where applicable.
- Current documented stable version: `jev-1.13.0`; aliases `jev-latest` and `jev-preview` currently point to it.
- Direct API: `POST /v1/systemone`. This is an evaluation API, not a chat-completions API.
- Official price checked today: $42 per billion input tokens, equivalently $0.042 per million. Outputs are free. The official model page documents a 64k request limit and additional 32k state-plus-longest-question limit. Pricing and limits can change.
- GitHub’s current Copilot list does not include Jev. Copilot Auto routes only among supported and policy-eligible chat models.
- VS Code MCP servers add tools. They do not automatically replace the selected chat model.
- VS Code custom endpoints support Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs. Jev’s evaluation API does not match those chat interfaces.
- TypeSafe’s official agent skill teaches agents how to build TypeSafe integrations. It is not an MCP server.

## Integration routes

### Supported components

1. Keep a normal Copilot-supported host model selected.
2. Use VS Code’s documented MCP support to connect a trusted local or remote tool server.
3. Have that tool call TypeSafe’s documented API with state and typed questions.
4. Keep policy, thresholds, deterministic checks, and side effects in application code.

The components are documented, but their composition into a Jev–VS Code workflow was not tested in this research.

### Community implementation to inspect

`jkudish/jev-mcp` is a community repository whose current README calls it early software. The README says it provides ten judgment tools, documents Node 20+, `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, and a local `npx` launch. Three examples from those ten are:

- `jev_verify`: compare claims with supplied evidence.
- `jev_screen`: screen text for prompt injection, substance, and relevance.
- `jev_find`: rank candidates against a query.

The repository provides a generic “Any other MCP client” configuration. Do not assume that its exact JSON is the current VS Code schema; add it through VS Code’s documented MCP workflow if evaluating it. Review and pin source first. It is not in the `typesafe-ai` GitHub organization and was not presented in TypeSafe’s official documentation index as an official server. No integration was installed or tested for this episode.

### Custom wrapper

A minimal custom MCP wrapper around `POST /v1/systemone` is technically plausible and gives control over the tool schema, payload filtering, logging, version pinning, and thresholds. This is a proposed architecture, not a tested integration. It adds maintenance and should only be built after a direct API pilot demonstrates value.

## Pilot recommendation

Use one bounded, reversible lane such as issue triage or research-result scoring.

- Dataset: at least 200 previously resolved examples plus a held-out test set.
- Pin: model version, prompt/rubric version, thresholds, and tool implementation commit.
- Baselines: deterministic rules; current small model with structured output; Jev; Jev plus low-confidence escalation.
- Metrics: task accuracy, per-class precision/recall, confidence calibration, costly false positives, review rate, end-to-end latency including host/tool round trips, total cost, timeouts/errors, and drift.
- Safety: no automatic high-impact action; deterministic validation before side effects; review ambiguous and adversarial examples.
- Adoption gate: a material quality, cost, or latency win after integration overhead. Schema validity alone does not count.

## Caveats and risks

- “No hallucinations” is a vendor framing for schema-constrained output. It does not establish correct decisions.
- In TypeSafe’s dated Sep 15 launch article, the “Workflow evals” and “Nuance” sections say the evaluations use predictions from large external models as reference probabilities rather than independent ground truth; the vendor also acknowledges possible bias and says its largest speed/cost gains are at the high end of real-world gains.
- A community study author reported 22/25 (88%) relevance and 24/25 (96%) credibility on 25 hand-authored, search-result-shaped items across four research goals. It was one sequential run with one person-session’s labels, an unpinnable gateway model version, and two label/rubric divergences. Treat it as a smoke test: it was not independently reproduced and was not a sampled live-search benchmark.
- Additional TypeSafe calls mean separate billing, credentials, network latency, rate limits, and availability.
- TypeSafe’s privacy policy says input is collected and not used to train or fine-tune models; retention is described broadly, while zero-data-retention is an enterprise offering. Assess before sending private code or records.
- VS Code warns that local MCP servers can run arbitrary code. Review publisher and configuration before starting one.

## Primary sources

1. TypeSafe introduction — https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.md
2. Jev with coding agents — https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents.md
3. Models and pricing — https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md
4. Jev 1.13 jaggedness — https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md
5. API reference — https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md
6. Launch post and vendor benchmark nuance — https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev
7. Official TypeSafe agent skill — https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill.md
